tier_reason: No numbers anywhere reachable: the README only says the library aims to be 'efficient' and cites three papers without results, and benchmarks/ holds only a nanobench harness (experiment.hpp, generators.hpp, module/{algorithm,combinatorial,core,math,special}) with no committed result tables. The cited papers (PACT 2012, HPCS 2018) and the github.io docs are unreachable here, so D stands.

corrections.caveats: No benchmark numbers in the README or repo; benchmarks/ has only the nanobench harness (CMakeLists.txt, experiment.hpp, generators.hpp, nanobench.h, module/ with algorithm, combinatorial, core, math and special subdirectories) and no result tables. The README calls EVE a research project first, with API and minimum compiler subject to change before a 0.1 release, and says some performance issues may remain. Documentation and the cited papers (PACT 2012 Boost.SIMD, HPCS 2018 small matrix-vector, Scalable Computing EVE article) live on github.io, ACM and HAL pages that were blocked here. Lead for a retier: Felix Rocke's April 2023 LMU bachelor thesis 'Evaluation of C++ SIMD Libraries' benchmarks six SIMD libraries against intrinsics on AVX2, AVX-512, SVE and NEON (abstract, snippet only: several libraries matched intrinsics, Highway strongest on the integer case study); whether EVE is among the six was not confirmed (nm.ifi.lmu.de blocked). Requires C++20 (g++ 13+, clang++ 16+, MSVC 19.44+); no dynamic-size SVE.

notes: Repo checked on github.com: BSL-1.0, 1.4k stars, not archived or a fork, last commits 2026-10-11, so metadata holds. Kept at D as a notable (1.4k stars) successor of Boost.SIMD with no published numbers; shortcoming: no benchmark results and no comparison against scalar code, Highway, xsimd or std::simd anywhere reachable. Retier lead: the 2023 LMU thesis (rock23.pdf) and the CppCon 2021 talk.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PVLDB 15 (2022) demo paper whose abstract (search snippet only) reports beating previous Web data libraries on TPC-H at several scale factors, with the paper's harness public in packages/benchmarks/src/suite_system_tpch_{duckdb,sqljs,arquero,lovefield}.ts; plus an independent repo (timlrx/browser-data-processing-benchmarks, public code, CPU and browser stated) whose Chrome table matches the claimed numbers. Not A: wasm build flags of the prebuilt npm bundles are not stated and the paper's CPU and results could not be opened.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Independent repo (timlrx/browser-data-processing-benchmarks README; times in seconds, Date.now() difference / 1000 in index.js), i7-1165G7 with Chrome 116: Test 1 top-level metrics Arquero 0.067 s vs DuckDB-Wasm 0.014 s (4.8x, derived from page data); Test 2 group by day 1.05 s vs 0.163 s (6.4x, derived from page data); Test 3 top 5 countries 4.847 s vs 0.114 s (42x, derived from page data); Test 4 10 random rows 0.517 s vs 0.032 s (16x, derived from page data). Against in-memory SQLite WASM without indexes DuckDB-Wasm also wins Tests 1-4 (e.g. Test 1 0.376 s vs 0.014 s, 27x, derived from page data). On the M2 MacBook Air with Firefox 117 the Arquero gaps are smaller (Test 3 0.852 s vs 0.132 s, 6.5x; Test 2 0.634 s vs 0.169 s, 3.8x; derived from page data). DuckDB-Wasm loses the load step (4.309 s vs Arquero 2.866 s and SQLite 0.893 s on Chrome), loses to indexed SQLite on Tests 2 and 4 (0.005 s and 0.002 s vs 0.163 s and 0.032 s), and loses every transactional test to in-memory SQLite WASM (1000 indexed selects 1.048 s vs 0.054 s, 1000 inserts 1.397 s vs 0.041 s, 1000 deletes 2.376 s vs 0.035 s). VLDB 2022 paper abstract (search snippet only): outperforms previous data processing libraries for the Web on TPC-H at multiple scale factors; no figures seen.
corrections.caveats: The VLDB PDF (vldb.org), duckdb.org and ir.cwi.nl were not reachable (DNS-blocked here); the paper claim comes from a search snippet, though the repo's packages/benchmarks/src holds TPC-H suites for DuckDB-Wasm, sql.js, Arquero and Lovefield that match the snippet's comparison set. The independent repo (7 stars, 23 commits) is a single run per browser on one machine, timed in seconds with Date.now() around a Comlink call to a web worker (so worker messaging and 1 ms clock resolution are included in the 0.002-0.03 s rows); its README says fetch and load timings are noisy. It pins old packages (@duckdb/duckdb-wasm ^1.27.0, @sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm ^3.43.0-build3, arquero ^5.2.0, 2023), and the workloads are not identical: the Arquero group-by-day test also sorts its output, which the DuckDB query does not. DuckDB-Wasm is slower to load than Arquero and SQLite and far slower than SQLite WASM on point lookups, updates, inserts and deletes; its wins are analytical scans and aggregations. No comparison against native DuckDB (the category's 'same library compiled natively' baseline) was found. Default build is single-threaded; multithreading is experimental.

notes: Numbers verified against the timlrx README tables and harness (index.js, benchmarks/duckdb.js, benchmarks/arquero.js); unit is seconds. Metadata holds (MIT, 2.1k stars, last commit 2026-09-29). Shortcomings to record: slower load than Arquero and SQLite, loses all transactional and indexed point-lookup tests to SQLite WASM, independent repo is a 7-star single-run harness on 2023 package versions, VLDB paper figures unseen (snippet only), no native-DuckDB comparison.

tier_reason: dmonad/crdt-benchmarks is the widely used independent CRDT shootout, maintained by the Yjs author (the competitor ran it), with public harness code (benchmarks/loro/factory.js, js-lib) and CPU (i5-8400) and Node 20.5.0 stated; every claimed number is in loro's column of its N=6000 table. Not A because the wasm build flags of the prebuilt loro-crdt 0.10.1 npm package are not stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: dmonad/crdt-benchmarks README, N=6000, i5-8400, Node 20.5.0, loro 0.10.1 vs yjs 13.6.11: B4 apply real-world editing dataset 3,089 ms vs 5,714 ms (1.85x, derived from page data); B4x100 309,689 ms vs 608,908 ms (2.0x, derived from page data); B4 parseTime 13 ms vs 39 ms; B1.1 append N characters 120 ms vs 188 ms; B1.4 79 ms vs 131 ms; B1.5 82 ms vs 154 ms; B3.1 56 ms vs 75 ms. Mixed: Yjs is faster on B2.2 (65 vs 83 ms), B2.3 (85 vs 112 ms), B2.4 (178 vs 208 ms), B3.3 (86 vs 116 ms), B3.4 (72 vs 227 ms) and trivially on B1.6, B1.9 and B2.1; Loro's encodeTime is far higher (B4 77 ms vs 11 ms, B4x100 14,429 ms vs 365 ms, B2.4 233 ms vs 12 ms), its documents are larger (B4 258,228 vs 159,929 bytes) and its bundle is 15x larger (1,052,250 vs 69,124 bytes; 399,276 vs 20,100 gzipped).
corrections.caveats: Third-party shootout maintained by the Yjs author, so the competitor ran it; wasm compiler flags are not stated. The results table is old: crdt-benchmarks' last commit is 2024-02-12 and the table measures loro 0.10.1 (now 1.x) and ywasm 0.9.3. The harness uses Loro's snapshot export by default (exportSnapshot stores the in-memory state, which lowers parseTime but enlarges docSize and encodeTime) and batches cached remote updates with importUpdateBatch inside a transaction. memUsed excludes wasm runtime memory, so Loro's 0 B rows are not comparable with Yjs's JS heap figures. Gains are workload-specific: Yjs wins most concurrent-conflict text/array workloads (B2.2-B2.4, B3.3, B3.4), all encode times and bundle size.

notes: Numbers verified in loro's column of the crdt-benchmarks README and the harness (benchmarks/loro/package.json pins loro-crdt ^0.10.1, factory.js uses exportSnapshot). Metadata holds (MIT, 6.2k stars, last commit 2026-10-09). Shortcomings to record: table measured 0.10.1 and is stale since 2024-02-12, Yjs wins most conflict workloads, encode time, doc size and bundle size; snapshot mode favors parseTime; memUsed ignores wasm memory.
